title: Storms from safety
hookLine: thunder and wind, heard from a safe place, can be awe instead of fear

lines: THE SAFER YOU ARE, THE MORE YOU SEE.
cards: Hail drums on a car roof. The driver has pulled in under a gas station canopy and switched off the engine. Nobody can hear the radio.
Across the road, the gutters have turned into streams and the trees are bending almost flat. Ten minutes ago, out on the highway, this storm was a gray wall and two hands tight on the wheel.
Now, under a roof, it's something to watch. That's the strange thing about storms: the safer you are, the more of their size you can take in.

teach.h: PSALM 29: THE GOD OF GLORY THUNDERETH.
teach.b: First, a storm with a voice in it. Psalm twenty-nine listens to a thunderstorm and calls the thunder a voice. In the King James words: "The voice of the LORD is upon the waters: the God of glory thundereth."
The voice breaks the cedars and shakes the wilderness. In this song, the storm itself is where the voice speaks. Second, a storm with no voice in it.
In the First Book of Kings, the prophet Elijah, worn out and hiding in a cave, is told to stand on the mountain.
A great wind tears at the rocks, "but the LORD was not in the wind." Then an earthquake, then a fire, and the LORD was not in those either.
And after the fire, "a still small voice." Third, both at once. These two texts don't cancel each other.
In one, the storm is where the voice speaks; in the other, the voice comes after the storm has passed.
A storm can be a messenger, or the loud thing that makes the quiet afterward audible. Fourth, why safety matters. Awe sits close to fear.
Out in a real storm, fear wins; the body is busy surviving.
Give it a roof, a window, a blanket, and there's room for the other feeling: how vast the sky is, how small a house is, how much power moves through a single gust.

how: In the Bible, Psalm 29 hears the voice of the LORD in the thunder, and Elijah hears a still small voice after wind, earthquake and fire; some people make a quiet practice of listening to storms from a safe place.

games.q: you're Elijah on the mountain. a great wind, then an earthquake, then a fire. where does the text say the LORD is?
o: in none of them: then comes a still small voice.
games.why: 1 Kings 19: the LORD was not in the wind, nor the earthquake, nor the fire. "and after the fire a still small voice."

practice: Listen to rain or wind from somewhere safe and dry, by a window open a crack or at the door; if it's calm out, play a recording of a storm, or remember one you heard from inside.
Notice how each gust swells and fades, and then the quiet underneath it. If you pray, you can listen for the still small voice; if you don't, let the storm be big while you are safe.

wordCard.voice: Elijah. The prophet who heard no voice in the wind, the earthquake or the fire, but a still small voice after the storm had passed. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew, 1 Kings 19:12: the phrase the King James renders "a still small voice".
